examples.problem_statement: Write the first five terms in the expansion of (a + b)^{-3}, |b| < |a|.

solution.description: Start from the generalized binomial theorem, which extends the ordinary expansion to any exponent n, including a negative one, at the price of the sum running on forever. The coefficient is written as a falling product divided by k factorial, because the familiar factorial form has no meaning once n is negative.

Substitute n equal to negative 3 into that general series. Every term now carries a power of a of the form negative 3 minus k, which is the same as 1 over a raised to 3 plus k, so successive terms push more and more of a into the denominator.

solution.operation: Calculate binomial coefficients for k = 0 to 4
solution.description: Evaluate the first five coefficients by taking k successive factors starting at negative 3 and dividing by k factorial. Each new factor is negative, so the signs flip term by term, and the sizes come out as 1, 3, 6, 10 and 15.

Attach each coefficient to its matching powers: the term for index k is that coefficient times a to the negative 3 minus k times b to the k. This is the expansion written out in full, still carrying negative exponents.

Move every negative power of a down into a denominator so all exponents become positive. The alternating coefficients from the previous step now show up as alternating plus and minus signs across the five terms.

Check the finished series against what the theory predicts: the signs alternate beginning with a positive term, and the coefficients 1, 3, 6, 10, 15 are the triangular numbers, which is exactly the pattern an exponent of negative 3 should produce. The expansion is only meaningful while b is smaller in size than a.

key_reminders: {'point': 'Note: Expansions for non-positive integer n are valid only when |b| < |a|.'}
{'point': 'See Problems 15.5–15.8 for practice.'}
{'point': 'Cross-reference: See Problem 15.3 for derivation context; See Problem 15.7(a) for verification of validity condition.'}
common_mistakes: Trying to compute the coefficient with the factorial formula n factorial over k factorial times n minus k factorial: with n equal to negative 3 there is no such factorial, so the falling-product form must be used instead.
Making every term positive. Each extra factor in the coefficient is negative, so the signs must alternate down the series.
Dropping the condition that b is smaller in size than a, under which alone this infinite expansion is valid.

examples.problem_statement: Find the area of a rectangular piece of land whose length and breadth are 7' 8'' and 5' 11'' respectively.

solution.description: The two sides are given in mixed units, so bring each to a single unit before multiplying: 7 feet 8 inches is 7 times 12 plus 8, that is 92 inches, and 5 feet 11 inches is 5 times 12 plus 11, that is 71 inches.

solution.description: With both sides in inches the area is the single product 92 times 71. Write the two numbers one above the other so the vertical and crosswise pairings can be read off the columns.
Multiply the units digits vertically, 2 times 1, which puts 2 in the units place of the area with nothing to carry.
Cross multiply for the tens column and add: 2 times 7 plus 9 times 1 is 23, so 3 stays in the tens place and 2 carries to the left.
Multiply the leading digits vertically, 9 times 7, giving 63, then fold in the carry of 2 from the previous column to make 65 for the left-hand part.
Read the columns left to right, 65 then 3 then 2, giving 6532 square inches as the area in the working unit.

examples.problem_statement: “In a certain investment, each rupee invested brings Rupees two and five annas to the investor. How much will an outlay of Rs. 4 and annas nine therein yield ?”

solution.result: 1 \text{ rupee invested} \rightarrow 2\text{ Rs. } 5\text{ As.} = 2\frac{5}{16} \text{ Rs.} = \frac{37}{16} \text{ Rs.}
solution.description: Read the rate first. Each rupee invested returns 2 rupees 5 annas, and since 16 annas make a rupee, 5 annas is 5 sixteenths of a rupee. The rate is therefore 2 and 5 sixteenths rupees, which as a single improper fraction is 37 sixteenths.

Put the sum invested into the same form: 4 rupees 9 annas is 4 plus 9 sixteenths, and writing the 4 as 64 sixteenths makes it 73 sixteenths of a rupee. Both quantities are now single fractions over the same denominator.

solution.operation: Multiply investment by yield rate using Vedic Math (Urdhva Tiryagbhyam)
solution.description: The yield is the amount invested multiplied by the rate, so multiply the two fractions: numerator times numerator over denominator times denominator. The numerator 37 times 73 is the one real multiplication in the problem and the crosswise sutra gives it as 2701 in a single line, over 16 times 16, that is 256.
Split the improper fraction back into whole rupees and a remainder: 256 goes into 2701 ten times with 141 left over, so the yield is 10 rupees plus 141 two hundred and fifty sixths of a rupee.

solution.operation: Convert fractional part to annas and pies
solution.description: Convert that leftover fraction of a rupee into annas by multiplying it by 16, because a rupee is 16 annas. The result is 2256 over 256, that is 8.8125 annas, so 8 whole annas with a fraction still to account for.
Take the fractional part of the annas, 0.8125, and multiply it by 12, because an anna is 12 pies. That gives 9.75 pies, or 9 and three quarters pies.
Money is quoted in whole pies, so the fraction of a pie is dropped and the yield reads 10 rupees, 8 annas and 9 pies, written in the customary form Rs. 10 dash 8 dash 9.
